idiom_name: typed predicates (candidate: T) => boolean and user-defined type predicates x is S
implementation_notes: TypeScript's contribution over JavaScript is the type: a rule is (candidate: T) => boolean, and when it also refines the type it is written as a user-defined type predicate, `(x: T): x is S`, which lets Array.prototype.filter and find narrow the result type through the rule. Parameterized rules are factories returning typed closures, composition is a small generic combinator, and the type predicate has an if-and-only-if contract that the compiler trusts without checking. A class-based Specification<T> with isSatisfiedBy is worth it only when rules must carry metadata (name, message) for logging or translation; the type system gives no runtime protection, so declared predicates that are not exact remain unsound and unnoticed.
pitfalls: A declared type predicate is an unchecked assertion: if the rule is not an exact if-and-only-if test, the narrowed type is a lie (TypeScript 5.5 infers predicates only for single-return boolean refinements).
Composition loses narrowing unless the combinator is generic over the predicate type; a boolean-returning wrapper erases the type guard at every call site.
Structural typing makes 'candidate' easy to over-widen: a rule typed against a whole entity is coupled to fields it never reads, so prefer minimal structural types.
As in JavaScript, a predicate passed to filter is in-memory evaluation; the query-side rule must be expressed separately in the data layer's dialect and kept consistent.
